description: A personal essay collection and structured knowledge graph mapping the three major Buddhist Abhidharma traditions (Theravāda, Sarvāstivāda, Yogācāra) onto contemporary frameworks in computational phenomenology — predictive processing, active inference, Global Workspace Theory, Parallel Distributed Processing, and related approaches. Comprises eighteen essays (nine themes × English + Japanese), a cross-tradition dharma comparison table (~130 dharmas across nine sheets), and a JSON-LD knowledge graph (316 nodes, schema.org + custom vocabulary) with bilingual labels and Sanskrit / Pāli / Chinese philological alignment. An interactive 2D/3D viewer is provided. v0.5.0 adds Theme 9 (On embodiment in the age of AI) — questioning the logical structure of the claim that AI lacks embodiment (The Blind Spot, 2024): from the process-structural view of mind shared by Abhidharma, Yogācāra and emptiness thought, input-data provenance (organic vs. digital sensors) draws no essential line; what does the theoretical work is the feedback loop (autopoiesis; Friston 2018 self-evidencing, structurally similar to Yogācāra's manas). Shows Buddhism itself splits on embodiment (only Theravāda posits the material heart-base hadaya-vatthu) and that defenders now stretch the concept (Froese 2026, distributed vs. organismic embodiment). First essay written as disclosed AI-mediated writing, carrying a machine-readable claims layer for LLM readers. Developed in collaboration with the Claude language model (Anthropic) for synthesis, cross-tradition mapping, and graph encoding; the author retains responsibility for all claims.
name: Attention, Not Self: Buddhist Abhidharma Meets Computational Phenomenology
